questions.stem: X-rays were accidentally discovered in 1895 while experimenting with cathode ray tubes. Which scientist made this discovery and later received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics?

options.option_text: Henri Becquerel, who discovered natural radioactivity in 1896
Wilhelm Röntgen, a German physicist and Nobel Prize winner
J.J. Thomson, who identified the electron using cathode rays
Ernest Rutherford, known as the father of nuclear physics

questions.explanation: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays on 8 November 1895 and won the inaugural Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. Henri Becquerel is the most tempting distractor because he discovered natural radioactivity in 1896, just a year later, and both discoveries relate to radiation — but Becquerel's subject was uranium, not cathode-ray experiments.

questions.stem: The first electric battery, called the 'voltaic pile', was invented in 1800. The SI unit of electric potential (voltage) is named after its inventor. Who was he?

options.option_text: André-Marie Ampère, pioneer of classical electrodynamics
Georg Ohm, who formulated the law of electrical resistance
Alessandro Volta, an Italian physicist and inventor (1800)
Michael Faraday, who discovered electromagnetic induction

questions.explanation: Alessandro Volta constructed the voltaic pile in 1800, the world's first device to produce a steady electric current. The unit 'volt' is named in his honour. Faraday is the most plausible distractor because he made foundational electrical discoveries, but his work on electromagnetic induction came three decades later (1831).

questions.stem: In 1816 a French physician invented the stethoscope by rolling paper into a cylinder after hesitating to place his ear directly on a patient's chest. Who was this physician?

options.option_text: William Harvey, who described the circulation of blood in 1628
Louis Pasteur, who developed the germ theory of disease
René Laennec, a French cardiologist and physician (Paris, 1816)
Joseph Lister, pioneer of antiseptic techniques in surgery

questions.explanation: René Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816 at the Necker Hospital in Paris by rolling sheets of paper into a tube. Louis Pasteur is the most tempting distractor because both are prominent 19th-century French medical scientists, but Pasteur's contributions were in germ theory and vaccines, not diagnostic instruments.

questions.stem: The theory of 'Continental Drift' — proposing that present continents were once joined as a single landmass called 'Pangaea' — was put forward in 1912 by which scientist?

options.option_text: Charles Lyell, the founder of modern geology and stratigraphy
Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist and geophysicist
James Hutton, who proposed the theory of uniformitarianism
Harry Hess, who explained sea-floor spreading in the 1960s

questions.explanation: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in his 1912 work 'The Origin of Continents and Oceans', introducing the concept of Pangaea. Harry Hess is a shrewd distractor: he provided the mechanism (sea-floor spreading, 1960s) that eventually validated Wegener's idea, leading students to confuse the two men's roles.

questions.stem: Which physicist discovered the neutron in 1932 by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles, thereby confirming the existence of the third fundamental subatomic particle?

options.option_text: J.J. Thomson, who discovered the electron using cathode rays
Niels Bohr, who proposed the planetary model of the atom
James Chadwick, a British physicist and 1935 Nobel laureate
Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the proton and atomic nucleus

questions.explanation: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 and received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935. Ernest Rutherford is the most tempting distractor because he predicted the neutron's existence around 1920 and discovered both the proton and the atomic nucleus — students often credit him with the discovery his own student completed.

questions.stem: The world's first synthetic organic dye, 'Mauveine', was accidentally produced in 1856 by an 18-year-old student who was actually trying to synthesise quinine to treat malaria. Who discovered it?

options.option_text: Friedrich Wöhler, who first synthesised urea in the laboratory
August Kekulé, who proposed the ring structure of benzene
Justus von Liebig, the founder of modern organic chemistry
William Henry Perkin, a young British chemistry student (1856)

questions.explanation: William Henry Perkin accidentally discovered mauveine at age 18 while working in his home laboratory, launching the entire synthetic dye and later the pharmaceutical industry. Kekulé is the most tempting distractor because his benzene ring structure (1865) also underpins organic dye chemistry, but the discovery of mauveine predates it by nearly a decade.

questions.stem: Radiocarbon dating — which determines the age of ancient organic materials by measuring the decay rate of the isotope Carbon-14 — was developed in 1949. Who developed this technique?

options.option_text: Ernest Rutherford, who studied radioactive decay and half-life
Frederick Soddy, who coined the term 'isotope' in chemistry
Willard Libby, an American chemist and Nobel laureate (1960)
Glenn Seaborg, who discovered several transuranic elements

questions.explanation: Willard Frank Libby developed radiocarbon dating at the University of Chicago in 1949 and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960 for this work. Ernest Rutherford is the canniest distractor: he established the concept of radioactive half-life and first measured it experimentally, making him an entirely plausible — but wrong — answer.
